source.title: NorBERTo: A ModernBERT Model Trained for Portuguese with 331 Billion Tokens Corpus
source.citation: Enzo S. N. Silva et al., 2026
source.authors: Enzo S. N. Silva; Pablo B. Costa; Raphael C. Vlasman; Rosimeire Pereira Costa; Henrique L. P. Silva; Lucas F. A. O. Pellicer; G. Rinaldo; Renato Almeida; D. Rabbani; Cinthya O. Oestreich; V. F. Caridá

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task scores for NorBERTo base and large variants, bearing on whether downstream performance improves with scale. It does not fit or test a predictive scaling law.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream task results, but no held-out pretraining cross-entropy losses, parameter/token/compute scaling fits, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal allocation results. Only downstream evaluations comparing model sizes are recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a corpus and model release paper. It trains two NorBERTo sizes (about 150M and 395M) and benchmarks them against other encoders. It never fits or tests a scaling relation. The base-vs-large difference is incidental: two points, different per-model hyperparameters, and best-of-HPO selection in the appendix. That cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in Limitations, to explain possible effects of smaller data exposure. The reader's 'tests/T2' for V6 overstates what the study does.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the emphasis is off. The authors conclude that modern architectures plus a large monolingual corpus improve Portuguese encoders without LLM-scale parameters. They note NorBERTo-base (150M) beats BERTimbau-large (340M) on several tasks. NorBERTo-large sets strong PLUE results and the best ASSIN 2 entailment F1 among the encoders evaluated, but no single model wins everywhere. 'Larger models generally achieve higher performance' is an appendix remark, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Portuguese masked-language-model encoders and evaluates fine-tuned downstream task scores. It does not use the original autoregressive pretraining-loss scaling measurement or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported downstream outcomes vary by task; NorBERTo-large does not improve over base on WNLI or FakeRecogna 2.0.

fits_no_version.finding: NorBERTo-large (395M) scores at or above NorBERTo-base (150M) on 8 of 10 downstream measures. WNLI is tied and FakeRecogna is marginally lower. Hyperparameters differ per size, and no uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A larger encoder trained on the same corpus usually scores higher on downstream tasks (two-point comparison, not a scaling law).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Computational Processing of Portuguese (PROPOR 2026)
record.problems: Only two NorBERTo sizes are compared for downstream task results; no scaling fit, uncertainty estimates, or held-out pretraining-loss measurements are reported. The similarity score of 0.766 is not assigned to a specific NorBERTo-large configuration in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant downstream comparison rows were left out.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss is reported against N, D or C.
All: the two sizes differ in both depth and width at different parameter counts.
All: no power-law fit in any regime.
Predictability with scale or loss: only two sizes are compared and no curve is fitted.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites the scaling-law originals only in Limitations. The study is better treated as not testing the claim. The reader's V6 supports/limits_scope labels are removed because a two-size comparison with per-model HPO cannot show predictable downstream scaling.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameter count, token count, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is reported.
The study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The study trains Portuguese text encoders but does not test whether scaling-law forms generalise to other modalities or training regimes.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance relationship or predictive/extrapolative downstream scaling curve is tested; comparisons cover only the reported task scores and model sizes.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or varied by setup or fitting choice.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ASSIN 2 entailment and semantic similarity; PLUE MRPC and RTE; TweetSent-BR, HateBR and TuPy-E
reader_labels.reason: The reported large-model scores exceed the NorBERTo-base scores on these downstream measures (R1–R5, R7–R9). These comparisons do not establish predictive extrapolation.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: WNLI is unchanged with the larger model, and FakeRecogna 2.0 is lower for the larger model (R6, R10); the study also does not test a predictive scaling curve.
